# 18-careforce — sources

Back-test entry `18-careforce.yaml`: Careforce, AI agents that call and book the patients a health center never reaches
(YC Fall 2024). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named.
"Author's choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the
Launch YC post of 2024-11-22 and the weeks around it (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later, and a later price sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Careforce - Must-have AI agents for Healthcare admin", 2024-11-22 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/MJj-careforce-must-have-ai-agents-for-healthcare-admin
- [YCP] YC company page, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/careforce
- [WB] careforce.ai in the Wayback Machine: snapshots of 2024-05-09 and 2024-05-18 (a near-empty page, no pricing), then none until 2025-11-13 — https://web.archive.org/web/20240518050058/https://careforce.ai/ ; index https://web.archive.org/cdx/search/cdx?url=careforce.ai
- [KFF] KFF Health News, Kern Family Health Care's Medi-Cal renewals with Careforce, 2026-08-04 — https://kffhealthnews.org/medicaid/medicaid-work-requirements-medi-cal-ai-agents-reenroll-careforce-california/
- [CHCF] California Health Care Foundation investment page (CHCF is an investor, $500,000, February 2026; the page blocks direct fetches, so the quote is as the diversity research recorded it) — https://www.chcf.org/investment/careforce/
- [SITE] careforce.ai, read 2026-10-22 (no pricing; /pricing returns 404) — https://careforce.ai/
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, medical assistants, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/medical-assistants.htm

No Launch HN exists (HN search for Careforce, read 2026-10-22: https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/search?query=Careforce&tags=story).

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Medical assistants at community health centers, who work the outreach lists between patients.
   [LYC] "For health centers & practices this means MAs (short-staffed with front desk and intake) end up spending most
   of their time on admin tasks and most patients are never outreached & scheduled for vital screenings/visits,
   leaving a 1/3rd of care unserviced." → `roles[assistant]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: of
   [LYC]'s three segments (health centers and practices; digital health and CCM companies; payers) the first, the one
   the post describes by its staff.

2. **What (the job).** Get every patient due for a screening or visit called and booked.
   [LYC] "Most care coordination & data sharing is still manually done by staff through phones, email, fax because of
   unintegrated systems and custom workflows too unique to automate out of the box." → `statements.problem`,
   `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** Each working day, when the list of due patients has to be called between patients.
   [LYC] "Outreach using 50+ editable scripts (mammograms, pre-post-op, onboarding etc.)"; "Leave Voicemails, Sending
   reminders, and autonomously retry patients as needed". → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: outreach call list`.
   Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (spec 120: a daily rhythm in a clinic read as working days) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; [LYC] gives no count. Prevalence `p_80_100` follows from "most patients are
   never outreached".

4. **Which people.** US community health centers (FQHCs) and primary-care practices that work outreach lists by phone.
   [LYC] "Our AI agents are already Live with health centers and digital health companies helping analyze, call,
   schedule, and generate revenue." → `context.segment`, `market: US` (a San Francisco company, [KFF]).

5. **Who pays.** The health center. [LYC] "Let us take on your calling, coordination, and manual admin work so you can
   get more patients in the door without burning out your staff."; "increase revenue with Careforce AI Agents".
   → `persona.decision_maker: {role: director}`. Author's choice: the decider is the health center's executive or
   operations director and the tested role "The CFO" (a second role, "The board", listed: FQHCs are governed by
   boards). Purchase friction's three items (a HIPAA security review — tested; giving the agent access to the EMR; a
   board vote) are the author's, from [LYC]'s "Use EMR, Scheduling, payer and provider portals through UI or API
   Integrations" and [KFF]'s note that plans "are responsible for ensuring that technology complies with state and
   federal regulations, including patient privacy and data security". Commitment's step, "try it on one outreach list":
   [LYC] "We'd love to learn about your use cases and give you personalized demos unique to your use case."; the
   wording is the author's.

6. **Mechanism.** Two agents: one calls, texts, emails and books; one pulls data and builds the lists.
   [LYC] "Careforce creates autonomous agents that are able to take on these human-glue tasks and complete them in the
   same way as your staff would without the need for integrations." [LYC] (Angelica) "Call, text, email, and schedule
   patients autonomously"; "Speak in 29 Languages to engage and educate across demographics"; "Make 100 calls / min.
   and finish a year's worth of outreach in weeks". [LYC] (David) "Prepare reports, and generate lists for Angelica to
   realize the unrealized revenue". → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`; Compatibility (the list straight out
   of the EMR — tested; open slots; patients picking up unknown numbers) and Adoption friction (hand the day's list to
   an AI caller — tested; take the calls it hands back, from [KFF] "This will always be, in my opinion, an AI-human
   combination"). Relative advantage's two benefits are [LYC]'s retries (fewer_attempts) and "finish a year's worth
   of outreach in weeks" (shorter_time); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** No price is public at launch or today: [LYC] offers demos, [WB] has no pricing page near launch,
   [SITE] has none today. The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$1,500 to $3,000 per health center a month**, is the
   operator's reading: a monthly per-site fee of the size community health centers pay for a part-time outreach caller's
   share of work (an MA's hour is about $22, [BLS]; $1,500 to $3,000 is roughly 70 to 135 such hours), set below what
   the bookings it claims to recover would bring in. It is said in `statements.commercial` as the founder would type
   it, and marked there and in the header as the operator's.
   Existing sacrifice, RATE about **30% to 33%** of the patients due for a visit or screening per health center a month,
   lost as "Visits and screenings never booked because nobody reached the patient": [LYC]'s "1/3rd of care unserviced"
   for health centers (33%) and "costing 30% in bookings" across healthcare (30%). Ability to pay is read `budget` by
   the engine (a percent of patients never compares with an amount a month), so the directors answer the budget item.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from [LYC]'s scripts list (mammograms, pre-post-op), the short-staffing it
   names, and [KFF]; no respondent is a real person. [KFF] (Kern's CEO) "But we are already stretched thin. We need this
   functionality to be much more effective and augment our efforts." [KFF] "In samples of actual conversations provided
   to a reporter, Angelica sounded lifelike at first, although more than once cross-talk with a patient caused the
   program to pause suddenly."

## Respondents → the public account each is based on

Medical assistants (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Yesenia Morales → [LYC] "short-staffed with front desk and intake"; the mammogram script from [LYC]'s scripts list.
- Thanh Nguyen → [LYC] "Speak in 29 Languages"; [KFF] a member who valued being called in Spanish; an MA who calls the Vietnamese-speaking patients herself is the author's.
- Keisha Robinson → [LYC] "most patients are never outreached & scheduled"; two staff out is the author's.
- Olga Petrenko → author's invention, filling a gap: a practice with a dedicated outreach coordinator whose list gets done, so the problem is not a chorus (against on Importance).
- Marisol Vega → author's invention: a chipped (rather_not_say) story, GUESSED by code.
- Darnell Hayes → author's invention: a vague, habitual story with no one occasion (GUESSED).
- Fatima Al-Sayed, Brandon Kealoha → author's invention: gate No (no outreach list worked in the window).
- Rosa Jimenez → [KFF] "it took her a minute before she realized she wasn't speaking with a human" and the cross-talk pauses, turned sceptical: older patients who hang up on a recording (Relative advantage negative).
- Abena Owusu → [LYC] "unintegrated systems" and [LYC] (David) "Use UI to download data across EMRs & portals"; a list built by hand fails the tested condition (Compatibility no).
- Priyanka Shah → author's invention, filling a gap: bookings into blocked slots, so she would not hand the list over (Adoption friction probably not).
- Miguel Ferreira → [LYC] "care coordination" staff; a care coordinator works the list (the Current-solution escape, someone_else_checks).

Health center directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Linda Okafor-Reyes, Harold Jensen → [LYC] "increase revenue" and "book 30% more appointments": directors who pay at the founder's band.
- Samuel Goldberg → author's invention: would pay above the band but tests first.
- Carmen Ruiz → author's invention: pays below the band until bookings are shown.
- Aisha Bello → author's invention, filling a gap: a health center booked out for weeks, so unbooked patients cost it nothing it counts (Nothing; would not pay).
- Richard Lam → [KFF] the privacy and data-security duty; a director who cannot say the cost or the price (both escapes).
- Nadia Haddad → [KFF] "an AI-human combination"; a pilot with staff listening in.
- Joseph Whitecloud → author's invention: outreach paid from grant money (taken from other spend), below the band.

The split on Price (4 of the 7 who name a rung at $1,500 or above) is the author's: no public account gives what a
health center would pay. No respondent carries the name of a customer, patient, official or founder in the sources.

## Status today

Same idea, traction moved to health plans. [SITE] still sells the two agents for payors, plans, FQHCs and specialties.
The public customers are Medi-Cal health plans doing renewal outreach: [KFF] "Kern Family has spent about $370,000 on the
software by Careforce, a San Francisco startup, to facilitate rapid and repeated outreach to members when it's time to
renew their coverage."; "estimated it would have had to spend $2.4 million in staffing costs to match the program's more
than 800,000 calls to its 387,000 members"; "Kern Family's Medi-Cal renewal rate in April was 94.9%". [CHCF] "With the
aid of Careforce, KFHC renewed 96% of their members during the first year, compared to 38% before using the AI platform."
[KFF] says the agent "speaks more than 30 languages" (29 at launch). Price today: not public.

## Could not be sourced

- **A price, at any time.** The founder's $1,500 to $3,000 per health center a month is the operator's reading (item 7);
  the only public money figure is one health plan's cumulative spend ([KFF], 2026), not a unit price.
- **A health center's share of patients never booked, measured.** The 30% to 33% are the founders' own launch claims
  (one for health centers, one for healthcare overall), not a study.
- **A buyer title.** [LYC] asks "Healthcare Orgs" for demos; the director as decider, the CFO and the board as the roles,
  and the three Purchase friction items are the author's.
- **First-person MA accounts.** None public; the occasions are scripted from [LYC] and [KFF] (a health plan, not a
  health center).
- **A launch-era site.** [WB] holds no snapshot between 2024-05-18 and 2025-11-13; the launch post is the only
  launch-era page. [CHCF] could not be fetched directly (a bot check); its quote is as the diversity research read it.
- An MA's hour: [BLS]'s median stands in; no cost in the entry is in hours.

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: The three answers make three different points -- show me bookings against a part-time caller, we have no open slots to fill, and grant money can't cover the price -- so leaving each on its own is how I'd read them, with no group they should have joined and no muddled names.
whys.g2: There is no junk on this line; all three answers speak plainly to what the tool would be worth to a health center.

whys.g1: All three answers ask to try it on their own patient list before buying, and Richard Lam's security review fits in as part of that same on-our-own-data trial, so one plainly named group is how a director would read them.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line, so nothing needed keeping out.

founder.order_why: The order mostly follows how I'd pitch Careforce, but screen 24 asks how directors should answer after the kicker already says the interviews are sent, when it belongs with screen 23 before anything goes out.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 4 carry the identical kicker and question, so the context step reads as being asked twice. Screen 22 (offer a pilot?) also largely repeats screen 20, since my first real step already is a pilot on one outreach list.
founder.missing: Nothing turns my cost answer (about 30-33% of due patients never booked) into money, such as what a booked visit or screening is worth to a health center, so that unbooked share can't be set against my $1,500-$3,000 a month and ability to pay falls back to a plain budget question.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: The 'One more thing' screen about what would take the time in buying sits between 5 of 6 and 6 of 6, interrupting the numbered run right before the final try-it question, when it belongs after the HIPAA question or at the end.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.asked_twice: Screens 7 and 8: the HIPAA security review time and 'what would take the time in buying Careforce' both ask how long buying would take
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: Whether it works with our EHR and phone system (Epic, NextGen, eClinicalWorks), how many medical assistants and patients per list we have, and whether it would help our UDS/HEDIS quality measures and value-based payer incentives, which is how I would justify the spend

screens.why1: Right after I typed what could slow a purchase, it makes sense to check the list Keel built from it before it becomes a belief to test.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the three things that could slow a purchase, it's obvious I now pick one to test and put a time on it.

screens.why4: By name, a Keel contact list, and one open link for a group are distinct and cover how I'd reach MAs and directors, and 'People I know by name' fits what I picked.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or my roles is changed or leaked; it only asks how the study goes out.
screens.instead: Who gets a link, the medical assistants and the health center directors? (pick for each) — People I know by name / People I found with Keel / One open link posted where they already are

screens.why_b1: The headline says 'People disagree' and cites Existing sacrifice's 4 of 7, but the page also says the verdict is the worst of all its cards, and two cards (Purchase friction, Commitment) did not hold, so the stated verdict does not match its own rule.
screens.why_b2: The stage page draws no chart, but each card's count line says plainly what was counted, over how many directors (7 or 8), and where the bar sits (5 of 7, 6 of 8, no more than 2 of 8), with how far short it falls.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment carry the exact lines I checked: director decides and CFO agrees, HIPAA review within about 6 weeks, try it on one outreach list now.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what this means for Careforce; the only statement explains who was asked, not that the HIPAA review timeline and the pilot commitment are the two things I have to fix before I can sell to health centers.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible and no card overstates, but the headline softens a stage with two failed beliefs into 'People disagree', which undersells how badly the money side went.
screens.instead: Did not hold: 2 of 6 beliefs failed among 8 directors. Half expect the HIPAA review to take longer than 6 weeks (bar: 2 of 8), and only 5 of 8 would try it on one outreach list now (bar: 6). Next, shorten the security review, for example with a ready HIPAA packet and a BAA, and make the first outreach list cheaper to say yes to.

screens.why_b1: "People disagree" sits right beside 4 of 7 at 30% or more against a bar of 5 of 7, one short, so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.

screens.why_b3: The 30% to 33% figure and "never booked because nobody reached the patient" are mine, but "health center directors already lose... per health center" is awkward wording: the center loses those bookings, not the director.
screens.why_b4: The So line repeats the count and points me to the Price card, but it doesn't say what the split means for me, for example that the loss is real at most centers but not at booked-out ones like Aisha's or lower-loss ones at 20% to 25%.
screens.why_b5: n is visible (8 answered, 7 counted), Aisha's zero and Richard's exclusion are explained, and "a small group: a lean, not a call" keeps it from overclaiming.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 directors lose 30% or more of due patients, 1 short of your bar; the 3 below lose 0% to 25%, so pitch first to centers that know their lists go uncalled, and check on the Price card whether the lower-loss ones still pay.

screens.why_b1: The verdict "People disagree" sits right beside the deciding count: 4 of 7 at $1,500 or more against a bar of 5 of 7, 1 short.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts each director's monthly price rung over 7 counted, my band is marked on its rung, and the bar sits at 5 of 7; all of that is plain at first look.

screens.why_b4: The So line repeats the count and sends me to the Insights tab instead of saying what this means for my pricing, though the quotes on the card (bookings proof, booked-out centers, grant-funded outreach) would have let it say so.
screens.why_b5: It flags the small group as "a lean, not a call" and keeps n visible, but "4 of 7 would pay your price" overstates a little: three of the four named $1,500 to under $2,500, so they may not reach the $3,000 top of my band.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 put it at $1,500 or more, but only 1 above $2,500, so the bottom of your band holds better than the top. The 3 short are a booked-out center and two who want bookings proof or pay outreach from grants. Lead at $1,500 with a bookings pilot. A small group: a lean, not a call.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 8 as you said or easier · bar 6 of 8 · at the bar', so I know my belief held and by exactly what margin.

screens.why_b3: 'Buyer and payer' and 'The health center director decides, and the CFO has to agree' are word for word what I checked on the way in.

screens.why_b5: The count line says all 8 answered and were counted and flags 'a small group: a lean, not a call', so a result sitting exactly at the bar is not dressed up as strong.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside "4 of 8 expect longer than 6 weeks · bar: no more than 2 of 8", so I see both the answer and the number that decides it.

screens.why_b4: It tells me to plan for a 6-weeks-to-3-months security cycle and points me to Insights for what eats the time, and the quotes (a demo on their own EMR with security people in the room, a month on one list) tell me what to bring.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside "5 of 8 said yes · bar 6 of 8 · 1 short", so I see the verdict and the deciding number together, and they agree.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts directors by their answer (5 yes, 2 probably not, 1 no) over 8, and the strip marks my bar at 6, so all three are plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: "Commitment" and "In most cases the health center director would try it on one outreach list now" are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates that 3 of 8 would not try it and sends me to Insights, without saying what the miss means for my pilot ask, such as offering a smaller first step or answering the privacy holdouts.
screens.why_b5: A flat "Did not hold" on a one-person miss out of 8 sits uneasily with the card's own "a small group: a lean, not a call", and the Ability to pay card said "Too few to call" in the same position.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict word (People disagree, Did not hold, Did not hold) with the deciding count and bar right beside it, e.g. 5 of 8 said yes · bar 6 of 8 · 1 short.
screens.why_b3: Price, Purchase friction and Commitment carry the belief lines I checked on the way in, word for word.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what to do next, such as offering a free month on one screening list or bringing booking numbers from a center our size; the themes hint at it but I have to work it out myself.
screens.why_b5: Counts stay visible on every line, the split on Price is called a disagreement rather than a hold, and the empty Commitment box says why it is empty (0 asked here, 2 asked on Price, 1 never saw it).

screens.why1: As the opening screener it makes sense to check first whether my health center calls patients off outreach lists before asking anything else.
screens.why2: Outreach lists and calling patients by phone are everyday words in a community health center, so I understand it on first hearing.
screens.why3: It asks whether I personally work the lists, but that is my medical assistants' job; as director I never dial those calls myself, so an honest answer from me is No even though my center does it every day.
screens.why4: Yes and No are clean, but my true answer, that my staff do it and I don't, has no place, so I either answer for my staff or get screened out.
screens.why5: The founder's segment phrase is carried over word for word and aimed at the person doing the calls, not at me, the director who pays, so the meaning drifts away from the decision-maker it should be reaching.
screens.why6: Heard aloud, it is one short question followed by yes or no, easy to answer at once.
screens.instead: Does anyone at your health center call patients from a list of those due for a screening or visit? Yes or no.

screens.why1: After the screener on outreach lists, showing me the idea before the buying questions is the obvious next step for someone who pays for our software.
screens.why2: EMR, payer portals and integration project are everyday words to me, but 'One AI agent ... The other' never says there are two agents, and 'Careforce, patients called and booked' is a fragment that doesn't say what the thing is, so I'd read it twice.
screens.why3: Getting due patients called and booked off our MAs' outreach lists is exactly what my center runs and what I'd be paying for.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: The product shown on purpose comes through, but the two-agent structure is half dropped and the first line doesn't say what Careforce is, so it has drifted a little from what was meant.
screens.why6: It is a long run of sentences heard once, with three lists ('calls, texts and emails', 'EMR or scheduling portal', 'EMR and payer portals'), and 'the other' dangles by ear with no 'two agents' to hang on.
screens.instead: Imagine Careforce, two AI agents for patient outreach. One builds your list of patients due for care from the EMR and payer portals; the other calls, texts and emails each patient in 29 languages, retries the ones who don't pick up, and books them in your EMR. The people building it believe it would do the calling the way your staff would, without an integration project.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking how many due patients we failed to book last month is the obvious way to size what the problem costs my center.
screens.why2: Patients due for a visit or screening and never booked is how I talk about our recall and care-gap numbers, so I can answer it on first reading.
screens.why3: I see care-gap and recall reports, but I don't track a monthly never-booked percentage, so I would be giving an educated guess from the dashboard rather than a number I know.
screens.why4: A percent box with None and I can't recall covers it, but None sits beside the escape as a second chip, and a director would naturally answer with a range more than one figure.
screens.why5: It still means getting every due patient called and booked, and nothing of the product or the founder's terms reaches me.
screens.why6: The question says well, but 'or a low and a high; none is 0' is a clipped clause that a listener has to unpack before answering.
screens.instead: Last month, about what share of your patients due for a visit or screening never got booked? Say a percent, or a rough range. Or say you can't recall.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the question on how many due patients go unbooked, asking what it would be worth to me is the obvious next step for the person who signs the checks.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but 'per health center' makes me stop: we run several sites under one health center, so I'd wonder whether they mean each clinic site or our whole organization.
screens.why3: I know our budget well, but 'patients called and booked' doesn't tell me if this is software my MAs use, an automated caller, or an outsourced call service, so I'd be partly guessing at the price.
screens.why4: The bands don't overlap, they run from small to large without gaps, 'I wouldn't pay for this' covers the no, and 'I can't say' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's pitch leaks to me, but the idea line is so thin that the price is no longer anchored to a clearly described product.
screens.why6: The two-step reading is easy to hold, but 'Or say you can't say' sounds clumsy aloud, and I'd hear 'per health center' with the same site-or-organization doubt.
screens.instead: Imagine Careforce, a service that calls your due patients and books them into open slots. What would it be worth to you a month, for each clinic site? Under $500 · $500 to under $1,500 · $1,500 to under $2,500 · $2,500 to under $5,000 · $5,000 or more · I wouldn't pay for this (escape: I can't say)

screens.why1: I just gave a monthly price, so asking where that money would actually come from is the obvious next thing a director gets asked.
screens.why2: It's plain to me, but 'a new budget line someone signed off' is missing its 'on', and 'There was no budget for it' switches to the past tense on a what-if question, so I'd read it twice.
screens.why3: Finding money for software is exactly my job, so I can answer this from what I do.
screens.why4: 'There was no budget for it' is in the past tense and doesn't say where the money would come from, and for a health center like mine grant money, such as HRSA or a quality-incentive pot, is a real source that only fits under 'new budget line' if I stretch it.
screens.why5: It's about paying for the tool at the price I gave, and nothing of the founder's plan or wording comes through beyond the name I was already shown.
screens.why6: The four options say well as a list, but 'Or say you can't say' is a clumsy echo out loud, and the spoken 'you already had' doesn't match the screen's 'we already had'.
screens.instead: If you went ahead at that price, where would the money come from? A budget line we already have · A new line someone would sign off on · A grant or incentive payment · Moved from other spending · There's no money for it — escape: I can't say

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I could sign off myself, asking how long our HIPAA security review would hold up the purchase is the obvious next step for a health center buying anything that touches patient data.
screens.why2: HIPAA security review is everyday language for me as a director, though 'before it went through' is a little loose because the review gets finished and the purchase goes through.
screens.why3: I know how long our compliance officer and IT take to vet a vendor and get a BAA signed, so I can answer this from experience.
screens.why4: The time bands run in order without overlap, cover everything from quick to over six months, include 'It wouldn't be needed', and 'I can't tell' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: The founder's step, a HIPAA security review, is asked as written, and nothing about the product's workings or the founder's roles leaks beyond the idea card I already saw.
screens.why6: Spoken, it is one short question with four options I can hold and one escape, then a simple either-or follow-up, and 'HIPAA' says easily.
screens.instead: If you bought Careforce, how long would your HIPAA security review take before you could sign? (same options)

screens.why1: Right after I said the HIPAA security review would take a while, it makes sense to ask what would slow the purchase down.
screens.why2: Short and plain; I can answer it right away in my own words.
screens.why3: I know what slows our purchases: the security questionnaire, the BAA, IT and the CFO signing off, and the board if it's big.
screens.why4: It's a box to type in, so there are no options to judge.
screens.why5: It uses the product name from the idea card and adds nothing new about the founder's plan.
